questions.title: Your Body Has a Governor
questions.question: In the Playbook, what does the nervous system's 'governor' care about above all?
options: How much horsepower you built in the weight room
How many reps you did today
questions.bookLine: A governor does not care how much horsepower you built in the weight room. It cares about one thing: survival.

questions.title: Why Strong Isn't Enough
questions.question: Why can a 'governed' athlete squat four hundred pounds and still not jump high?
options: The nervous system will not release the strength while it has flagged a vulnerability
questions.bookLine: The nervous system will not release it, because somewhere in the kinetic chain — at the ankle, at the hip, at the thoracic spine, in the breathing pattern — there is a structural vulnerability that the governor has flagged.

questions.title: The Sequence That Changes Everything
questions.question: What is the Playbook's four-step sequence, in order?
questions.bookLine: Assess → Correct → Load → Perform.

questions.title: What This Means for You Tonight
questions.question: A coach sees a lazy-looking lateral slide on film. What does the Playbook say not to default to?
questions.bookLine: If you are a coach and an athlete's lateral slide looks lazy on film, do not default to cone drills.

questions.title: The Pressure Cylinder
questions.question: Why does the Playbook say a youth athlete needs a hydraulic model of the trunk?
options: Every landing is a pressure event
It makes the spine more flexible
questions.bookLine: Because every landing is a pressure event.

questions.title: Cavity 1: The Cranial Vault (Your Head)
questions.question: What does forward head posture shorten, according to the Playbook?
options: The small muscles at the base of the skull (the suboccipitals)
questions.bookLine: Forward head posture — ear sitting clearly in front of the shoulder — shortens the small muscles at the base of the skull (the suboccipitals).

questions.title: Cavity 2: The Thoracic Cage (Your Rib Cage)
questions.question: When the rib V-angle opens wider than about 90 degrees, what is lost?
questions.bookLine: When the rib cage is flared — the V-angle where the bottom ribs meet at the breastbone opens wider than about 90 degrees — the ZOA is lost.

questions.title: Cavity 3: The Pelvic Basin (Your Pelvis and Floor)
questions.question: In the pressure cylinder, which part is the inferior (bottom) piston?
questions.bookLine: The pelvic floor is the inferior piston of the pressure cylinder.

questions.title: Your Breath Is the Control Dial
questions.question: Why does the Playbook call breath the control dial?
options: It is the only autonomic function you can also run on purpose
It is the fastest way to build muscle
It sets your heart rate directly
questions.bookLine: Breath is the only autonomic function you can also run on purpose.

questions.title: Force From the Ground Up
questions.question: To slide left, which way does the right foot push the ground?
questions.bookLine: To slide left, the right foot pushes the ground to the right.

questions.title: The Foot Tripod
questions.question: What are the three points of the foot tripod?
options: Center of the heel, base of the first metatarsal, base of the fifth metatarsal
Big toe, little toe and ankle bone
Heel, arch and ball of the foot only
questions.bookLine: Three points of ground contact make a stable foot: the center of the heel, the base of the first metatarsal (the big-toe joint), and the base of the fifth metatarsal (the pinky-toe joint).

questions.title: Movement Snack: The Ankle Architecture Reset
questions.question: In the Single-Leg Oscillatory Pogo, what does a mushy or heavy bounce mean?
options: The arch collapsed and is absorbing energy instead of returning it
questions.bookLine: Mushy or heavy means the arch collapsed and is absorbing energy instead of returning it.

questions.title: Putting the Cylinder and the Ground Together
questions.question: An athlete foam-rolls for twenty minutes and still looks flat in the first step. What does the Playbook suggest instead?
options: Two minutes of tripod and short foot plus one minute of long-exhale rib resets
questions.bookLine: Two minutes of tripod and short foot plus one minute of long-exhale rib resets will usually beat passive rolling for court transfer.

questions.title: Why 5 Minutes Is Enough to Find the Problem
questions.question: The quick check treats the body as three building blocks stacked on what?
questions.bookLine: You need a fast visual system that treats the body as three building blocks — cranial vault, thoracic cage, pelvic basin — stacked on a foot-and-ankle foundation.

questions.title: The 5 Checks
questions.question: In Check 1, the Heel Line, where do you stand and what do you look at?
options: Behind the athlete, at the heel bone
At the side, at the ear
questions.bookLine: Stand behind the athlete. Look at the heel bone (calcaneus).

questions.title: Check 2: The Knee Window (view from the front)
questions.question: In Check 2, the Knee Window, what are inward-facing 'squinting kneecaps' a flag for?
questions.bookLine: Inward-facing kneecaps — ‘squinting kneecaps’ — are an ACL-risk flag and often trace back to the foot findings from Check 1.

questions.title: Check 3: The Hip Level Check (view from the front, waistline)
questions.question: In the Hip Level Check, how big a difference between the hip points is significant?
questions.bookLine: A difference of more than about one finger-width is significant.

questions.title: Check 4: The Rib Angle (view from the front, chest)
questions.question: In the Rib Angle check, what is the ideal angle of the V where the bottom ribs meet?
questions.bookLine: Ideal is roughly a 90-degree angle.

questions.title: Check 5: The Head Float (view from the side)
questions.question: In the Head Float check, the vertical line from the earlobe should pass through what?
options: The bony tip of the shoulder (the acromion)
questions.bookLine: That line should pass through the bony tip of the shoulder (the acromion).

questions.title: The Single-Leg Wobble Test
questions.question: In the Single-Leg Wobble Test, what is the headline finding?
options: A mild wobble on both sides
One side stable and the other failing
Holding for more than a minute
questions.bookLine: If one side is stable and the other fails, that asymmetry is your headline finding — more important than a mild bilateral wobble.

questions.title: What to Do With Findings
questions.question: With 1–2 red flags, what does the Playbook's triage say to do?
options: Keep training, but address the specific faults before you add intensity
questions.bookLine: 1–2 red flags: Keep training, but address the specific faults before you add intensity.

questions.title: How to Run This Before Practice
questions.question: How many athletes per practice does the Playbook suggest a coach screens?
questions.bookLine: Coaches: pick two athletes per practice to screen while the team foam-rolls or shoots free throws.

questions.title: Joint 1 — The Ankle
questions.question: What does the Playbook call the most common mobility deficit in basketball athletes?
questions.bookLine: Limited dorsiflexion is the most common mobility deficit in basketball athletes.

questions.title: Joint 2 — The Hip
questions.question: Restricted hip external rotation is a root driver of what?
questions.bookLine: Restricted hip external rotation is a root driver of defensive stance breakdowns — the athlete cannot sit into a wide base without the knees collapsing or the low back taking over.

questions.title: The Hip 90/90 Position — Mobility Home Base
questions.question: In the 90/90 position, which way is each hip working?
options: Front hip in external rotation, rear hip in internal rotation
Neither — it is a rest position
questions.bookLine: This loads both directions at once: the front hip is in external rotation, the rear hip is in internal rotation.

questions.title: Joint 3 — The Thoracic Spine
questions.question: How much thoracic rotation to each side does the Playbook call a reasonable expectation in a healthy athlete?
options: As much as the lower back allows
questions.bookLine: From the Blueprint's seated rotation screen: roughly 45 to 50 degrees of thoracic rotation to each side is a reasonable expectation in a healthy athlete.

questions.title: The 7-Minute Daily Joint Unlock
questions.question: How long is the Daily Joint Unlock, and what does it need?
questions.bookLine: Total: 7 minutes. No equipment. Any room.

questions.title: Why Static Stretching Before a Game Is the Wrong Call
questions.question: For how long after static stretching may force production be reduced, according to the Playbook?
questions.bookLine: The effect may persist for up to 30 minutes and varies by stretch duration and muscle group — treat it as a guideline rather than a universal rule.

questions.title: The 10-Minute Pre-Game Protocol
questions.question: What does the Playbook say about the order of the pre-game phases?
options: Run them in order — each phase sets up the next
Do only the ones you like
questions.bookLine: Run the phases in order. Do not shuffle them. Each phase sets up the next — release, pressurize, feet, joints, rhythm, launch.

questions.title: Phase 1: Release the Locks (2 minutes)
questions.question: Phase 1 clears the two most common tight spots before a game. Which two?
questions.bookLine: What it is: two quick contract-relax cycles for the two most common tight spots in athletes before a game — ankles and hip flexors.

questions.title: Phase 2: Pressurize the System (1 minute)
questions.question: In the Phase 2 IAP breath, how long is the exhale?
questions.bookLine: Exhale through pursed lips for six seconds — feel the ribs compress.

questions.title: Phase 3: Wake Up the Tripod (1 minute)
questions.question: In Phase 3, how long do you hold the short-foot activation?
questions.bookLine: Draw the big-toe base gently toward the heel without curling the toes (short foot activation). Hold three seconds.

questions.title: Phase 4: Open the Joints (2 minutes)
questions.question: What is Phase 4, Open the Joints?
options: Quick joint circles for ankles and hips, moving through range with intent
questions.bookLine: What it is: quick joint circles for ankles and hips — not stretching, just moving through range with intent.

questions.title: Phase 5: Build the Rhythm (2 minutes)
questions.question: In Phase 5's pogos, how much knee bend does the Playbook allow?
questions.bookLine: Begin bouncing on the balls of the feet — minimal knee bend (15 to 20 degrees max).

questions.title: Phase 6: Prime the Launch (2 minutes)
questions.question: How many rounds of the Jump Readiness Sequence does Phase 6 call for?
questions.bookLine: Three rounds is enough when each round is honest.

questions.title: How a Jump Actually Works
questions.question: Once you leave the floor, what sets your jump height?
options: Swinging your arms in the air
questions.bookLine: Height is set by vertical velocity at takeoff.

questions.title: Concept 1: The Countermovement Is Where the Jump Is Won
questions.question: What does the Playbook call the bigger gift of the countermovement?
options: Time for the nervous system to get online
questions.bookLine: The Blueprint is blunt here: the spring is real, but the bigger gift of the countermovement is time for the nervous system to get online.

questions.title: Concept 2: The 90-Degree Law for Approach Jumps
questions.question: In the 90-Degree Law, what should be at roughly 90 degrees when the plant foot owns the floor?
questions.bookLine: As a coaching law for youth athletes: the knee should hit roughly 90 degrees of flexion at the moment the plant foot owns the floor.

questions.title: What a Dangerous Landing Looks Like — and What to Listen For
questions.question: In a safe landing, in what order do the joints absorb force?
options: Ankle first, then knee, then hip
questions.bookLine: A safe landing absorbs force across three joints — ankle first, then knee, then hip.

questions.title: Drill 1: The Countermovement Geometry Check (60 seconds)
questions.question: In the Countermovement Geometry Check, how long do you hold the bottom position?
options: You don't hold it — you jump
questions.bookLine: Hold that position for three seconds.

questions.title: Drill 2: The Oscillatory Pogo Progression
questions.question: How long should the pogo base be built before high boxes or depth jumps?
questions.bookLine: Do not jump onto high boxes or do depth jumps without first spending two to four weeks building this base.

questions.title: Weeks 1–2: Bilateral Pogos (Both Feet)
questions.question: What do weeks 1–2 of the pogo progression prescribe?
options: Three sets of about 20 contacts, both feet
questions.bookLine: Carry Phase 5 of the warm-up into training sets: three sets of about 20 contacts, crisp pop sound, arms in opposition, no heel slap.

questions.title: Weeks 3–4: Unilateral Pogos (One Foot)
questions.question: What do one-foot pogos in weeks 3–4 expose immediately?
questions.bookLine: This exposes ankle weakness and asymmetry immediately.

questions.title: Drill 3: The Safe Landing Check
questions.question: In the Safe Landing Check, what do you step off, and how long do you hold the landing?
questions.bookLine: Safe landing check: step off a 12-inch box. Land softly, hold the landing position for 3 seconds without knee cave or forward trunk collapse.

questions.title: What Parents Should Watch on Film
questions.question: In the fifteen-minute driveway session, at what effort are the three countermovement jumps done?
questions.bookLine: then three submaximal countermovement jumps at seventy percent effort for pattern proof — not testing day.

questions.title: Why Ladder Drills Are the Wrong Starting Point
questions.question: What kind of problem does the Playbook say speed is?
questions.bookLine: Speed is a force problem.

questions.title: Drill 1 — The Wall Drive
questions.question: In the Wall Drive, where does the forward lean come from?
options: The ankles — the entire body, like a ramp
questions.bookLine: Lean your ENTIRE body forward from the ankles — not just the head and chest.

questions.title: Drill 2 — The 3-Step Decel
questions.question: In the 3-Step Decel, how far should the planted knee bend on landing?
options: Until the knee touches the floor
questions.bookLine: Let the knee bend deeply on landing — at least 90 degrees — and let the hip drop back and down simultaneously.

questions.title: Drill 3 — The Lateral Bound and Stick
questions.question: In the Lateral Bound and Stick, how long do you hold the single-leg landing?
questions.bookLine: LAND on the opposite foot. Single-leg landing. HOLD for two full seconds.

questions.title: Drill 4 — The T-Drill (No Cones Needed)
questions.question: How is the T-Drill laid out?
options: A marker 10 yards ahead, with markers 5 yards to its left and right
Four markers in a square, 5 yards apart
questions.bookLine: Place one start marker. Place one marker 10 yards straight ahead. Place one marker 5 yards to the left of the forward marker. Place one marker 5 yards to the right.

questions.title: Setup and Execution
questions.question: In the Resisted March to Sprint, what does the working athlete lean into?
questions.bookLine: The working athlete places their hands on the back of a partner's shoulders.

questions.title: Common Errors and Fast Fixes
questions.question: Lateral bounds are turning into diagonal hops with a falling stick. What is the fix?
options: Shrink distance until the stick is silent and balanced for two seconds
questions.bookLine: Fix: shrink distance until the stick is silent and balanced for two seconds.

questions.title: A 15-Minute Coach Script
questions.question: In the 15-minute coach script, what does the coach watch during the Lateral Bound and Stick?
questions.bookLine: Minute 6–10: Lateral Bound and Stick, six each way. Coach watches knees, not distance.

questions.title: The Developing Frame — Why Technique Comes Before Load
questions.question: Around what age do growth plates in adolescent athletes fully close?
questions.bookLine: The growth plates in adolescent athletes do not fully close until around 17–18 years old — often earlier for females, later for males.

questions.title: Movement 1 — The Hip Hinge
questions.question: In the bodyweight RDL, when do you stop lowering?
options: When your hands touch the floor
questions.bookLine: STOP before the lower back rounds.

questions.title: Movement 2 — The Split Squat
questions.question: Why does the Playbook favour the split squat for basketball?
options: It is easier than a squat
Basketball is a single-leg sport pretending to be a two-leg sport
questions.bookLine: Why it matters: basketball is a single-leg sport pretending to be a two-leg sport.

questions.title: Movement 3 — The Glute Bridge
questions.question: Why are most youth athletes' glutes inhibited, according to the Playbook?
questions.bookLine: Most youth athletes have significantly inhibited glutes from excessive sitting — the hip flexors shorten and neurologically quiet the glutes through reciprocal inhibition (when one muscle group tightens, its opposite group down-regulates).

questions.title: Glute Bridge with Pressure Cylinder
questions.question: In the Glute Bridge with Pressure Cylinder, when do you drive the hips up?
questions.bookLine: On the exhale, drive the hips UP by squeezing the glutes.

questions.title: Scapular-Controlled Push-Up
questions.question: In the scapular-controlled push-up, at what angle are the elbows?
options: Tucked tight like a military press
questions.bookLine: Elbows at about 45 degrees from the body (not flared wide like a T, not tucked tight like a military press).

questions.title: Breathing Plank
questions.question: What is the breathing rhythm of the Breathing Plank?
questions.bookLine: Take a full IAP breath cycle: 4 seconds in, 6 seconds out, without losing the brace.

questions.title: The Weekly Bodyweight Strength Template
questions.question: When does the template say to add load, bands or backpack weight?
options: Only when the bodyweight version is boringly solid
questions.bookLine: Do not add load, bands, or backpack weight until the bodyweight version is boringly solid — no shaking, full holds, matching left-to-right quality on split squats and single-leg bridges.

questions.title: Progressions Without a Weight Room
questions.question: In the split squat progression, when do light dumbbells come in?
options: Only after the elevated version is stable
questions.bookLine: light dumbbells only after the elevated version is stable.

questions.title: Where This Fits With Sport Practice
questions.question: Where does the Playbook say SAQ from Chapter 7 should go in the week?
options: Before grinding conditioning, on fresh legs
Right after a lower-body strength day
questions.bookLine: SAQ from Chapter 7 prefers fresh legs — put it before grinding conditioning, not after.

questions.title: Recovery Is When the Adaptation Happens
questions.question: Who does the Playbook say wins: six training days with poor recovery, or four with complete recovery?
questions.bookLine: An athlete who trains six days a week and recovers poorly will be outperformed by an athlete who trains four days a week and recovers completely.

questions.title: Your Breath Is the Switch — Sympathetic to Parasympathetic
questions.question: Which kind of breathing biases the system toward parasympathetic activation?
options: Apical breathing — high chest and shoulders
Diaphragmatic breathing — belly first, then 360-degree rib expansion
questions.bookLine: Diaphragmatic breathing — belly first, then 360-degree rib expansion — stimulates the vagus nerve pathway and biases the system toward parasympathetic activation.

questions.title: Protocol 1 — The 4-6 Recovery Breath
questions.question: In the 4-6 Recovery Breath, why is the exhale longer than the inhale?
options: The longer exhale is the parasympathetic nudge
questions.bookLine: Make the exhale longer than the inhale. The longer exhale is the parasympathetic nudge.

questions.title: Protocol 2 — The Pre-Sleep Wind-Down
questions.question: When does the Pre-Sleep Wind-Down start?
options: After you are in bed with the lights off
questions.bookLine: Timing: start this routine 20–30 minutes before intended sleep time.

questions.title: Step 1 — Technology Off
questions.question: How long before the wind-down routine do screens go off?
options: They can stay on for the alarm
questions.bookLine: Screens off 10 minutes before this routine begins.

questions.title: Step 2 — Legs Up the Wall (5 minutes)
questions.question: How long do you stay in Legs Up the Wall?
questions.bookLine: Stay for 5 minutes.

questions.title: Step 3 — Supine Spinal Twist (2 minutes each side)
questions.question: In the Sleep Breath, how do you exhale?
questions.bookLine: Exhale through the nose (not the mouth) for 6–8 seconds.

questions.title: Protocol 3 — The Sleep Quality Checklist for Parents
questions.question: How often should parents run the Sleep Quality Checklist?
questions.bookLine: Audit weekly.

questions.title: Why Sleep Matters for Athletic Development
questions.question: When does growth hormone secretion peak?
questions.bookLine: Growth hormone secretion peaks during deep sleep.

questions.title: Tournament and Back-to-Back Days
questions.question: Between two games on the same day, how many rounds of 4-6 breathing does the Playbook suggest?
questions.bookLine: Use 6–8 rounds of 4-6 breathing in a quiet chair, sip water, light snack if timing allows, then a short reactivation from Chapter 5 before tip — feet, hips, cylinder, two light jumps.

questions.title: Troubleshooting the Protocols
questions.question: If the 4-6 breath makes an athlete anxious, what does the Playbook suggest?
options: Shorten the exhale to five seconds for a week and sit instead of lying down
Lengthen the exhale to ten seconds
questions.bookLine: If the 4-6 breath makes the athlete anxious, shorten the exhale to five seconds for a week, keep the nasal inhale, and sit instead of lying down.

questions.title: A Note to Athletes Who Think Recovery Is Soft
questions.question: How does the Playbook reframe recovery for hard workers?
options: A loophole for people who can't handle drills
How you earn the right to train hard again tomorrow
questions.bookLine: Recovery is how you earn the right to train hard again tomorrow with a nervous system that still trusts you.

questions.title: Section 1 — The Red Flags: What to Watch For
questions.question: What does the Playbook ask a parent to do with a red flag?
options: Recognize the flag and ask questions
Pull the athlete from the team
questions.bookLine: You do not need to diagnose the problem. You need to recognize the flag and ask questions.

questions.title: Red Flag 1 — Pain Is Normalized
questions.question: Which of these does the Playbook say is NOT normal soreness?
options: A dull ache 24–48 hours after a hard session
questions.bookLine: Sharp pain during movement, joint pain, or pain that persists beyond 72 hours is not.

questions.title: Red Flag 2 — No Mobility or Movement Prep Before Intensity
questions.question: About how long does the Chapter 5 pre-game protocol take?
questions.bookLine: The pre-game protocol in Chapter 5 takes about 10 minutes.

questions.title: Red Flag 3 — Heavier in Training Than in Games
questions.question: In-season, what does general sports science support doing with training volume?
options: Reducing it relative to the off-season while maintaining intensity
questions.bookLine: General sports science consensus supports reducing total training volume in-season relative to the off-season — maintaining intensity while cutting volume allows performance to peak at competition while managing cumulative tissue load.

questions.title: Red Flag 4 — Single-Sport Specialization Before Age 14 Without Physical Preparation
questions.question: Year-round single-sport training below what age is associated with more overuse injury and burnout?
questions.bookLine: Year-round single-sport training in athletes younger than 14 is associated with higher rates of overuse injury and burnout.

questions.title: Red Flag 5 — The Athlete Stops Enjoying the Sport
questions.question: An athlete who loved the game becomes reluctant to go to practice, with no obvious reason. What does the Playbook say it may be?
questions.bookLine: This is not a motivational failure. It is a physiological signal.

questions.title: Red Flag 6 — Rapid Technique Degradation Late in Sessions or Games
questions.question: What does late-session technique breakdown mean, according to the Playbook?
options: The athlete has exceeded their technical training capacity
questions.bookLine: Form breakdown late in a session — knee caving in, back rounding on hinges, arm swing disappearing, landings getting loud and stiff — means the athlete has exceeded their technical training capacity.

questions.title: Section 2 — Questions to Ask Any Coach
questions.question: What do a coach's answers to precise questions tell you more about than the facility tour?
questions.bookLine: The answers tell you more about program quality than the facility tour or the win-loss record.

questions.title: Section 3 — Training Load Management
questions.question: What should training load match, according to the Playbook?
options: What the athlete's nervous system can currently express with good technique
questions.bookLine: What appropriate training volume looks like for ages 13–18 starts with one principle: load should match what the athlete's nervous system can currently express with good technique — not what a fixed calendar PDF demands.

questions.title: Weekly Volume Guideline (Starting Reference)
questions.question: In-season, about how many hard strength/power sessions a week does the starting reference cap?
questions.bookLine: Cap total hard strength/power sessions around 4–5 off-season and about 3 in-season — assuming 8–10 hours of sleep and solid nutrition.

questions.title: How to Talk to Coaches Without Starting a War
questions.question: How does the Playbook suggest opening a conversation with a coach?
questions.bookLine: Lead with observation, not accusation.

questions.title: Multi-Team Math
questions.question: If the monthly calendar shows four high-intensity days in a row, what should happen?
options: Something becomes a technical day, a mobility day, or a rest day
Move them all to the weekend
questions.bookLine: If you see four high-intensity days in a row, something has to become a technical day, a mobility day, or a rest day — even if a fee already paid makes that emotionally hard.

questions.title: Your Role as the Architect
questions.question: What is the one thing the Playbook says no book can give your athlete?
questions.bookLine: The one thing no book can give your athlete is consistency.
